paragraphs: This checklist supports self-questioning only. It does not constitute hiring criteria, an ability score, or a conclusion about service quality or food safety. This page follows US O*NET-SOC 35-3023.00, Fast Food and Counter Workers (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese name for fast food and counter workers; the main work involves taking orders, serving food and beverages at counters or steam tables, collecting payment, and possibly preparing simple food and beverages).

Practice prompt | A fast food shop needs counter service during a completely fictional lunch rush (12 people queuing and delayed kitchen orders). Write a service and food safety proposal covering: (1) taking orders in sequence and repeating them for confirmation (including additions, no ice, and allergen alerts); (2) assembling and packaging meals and checking orders (main items, drinks, sides, and utensils); (3) operating the register, giving change, and reconciling end-of-shift accounts; (4) controlling hot-food and cold-drink temperatures and service time limits and preventing cross-contamination (separating raw and cooked food, changing gloves, and cleaning surfaces); and (5) responding to customers chasing orders and complaints and escalating beyond your authority. Use public information and simulated data; do not use real customer, shop, or payment information.

Fit signals | O*NET highlights: constant contact with others (89% constant contact), teamwork being extremely important (86%), daily face-to-face discussions with customers and colleagues (62%), daily in-person handling of unpleasant or emotionally upset customers (78%), considerable decision freedom (73%), exactness or accuracy being extremely important (50%), repeating the same tasks being extremely important (54%), coordinating or leading others being extremely important (42%), and continually or almost continually performing repetitive motions (64%) and standing (54%). If you remain steady at a fast pace and during peaks, willingly follow standard procedures and communicate frequently with customers, and enjoy teamwork, this occupation's daily demands are closer to your working style.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows daily contact with unpleasant, angry, or discourteous people (78%), daily exposure to minor burns, cuts, or punctures (29%), bending or twisting about half the time (57%), continual or almost continual repetitive motions (64%) and standing (54%), very close physical proximity (48% very close), conflict more than weekly (42%), and high time and service pressure. Work commonly includes early and late shifts, weekends, and holidays, requiring prolonged standing, moving goods, cleaning and dishwashing, and compliance with food safety and hygiene procedures. If customer conflict, prolonged standing, and repetitive work are difficult, or early, late, and holiday shifts do not suit you, weigh these practical costs carefully.

Responsibility judgment | Real fit depends on whether you can accomplish three things together at peak shop pace: maintain standard service (repeat orders, check assembly, take accurate payments, and serve on time), ensure food safety (temperature and time controls, raw and cooked separation, cleaning and hygiene), and take responsibility for reviewable records while working with customers and colleagues (orders, cancellations, end-of-shift accounts, and abnormality reports). Test this through a verifiable experience, such as peak-period fast food assistance, food safety and hygiene training with practical assessment, or a simulated counter service exercise, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire.

Safe work sample (a completely fictional task package): Given a simulated fast food lunch rush (12 people queuing, delayed kitchen orders, and one allergen note), complete a counter service and food safety proposal within 60 minutes: order and confirmation records (including additions, no ice, and allergen alerts), assembly and packaging checklist, payment and end-of-shift reconciliation records, temperature and time control plan (hot holding, cold-drink refrigeration, raw and cooked separation, and glove changes), and cleaning and surface-disinfection arrangements. Specify situations requiring a pause and escalation rather than handling them yourself, such as suspected allergen cross-contact, equipment failure, intense customer conflict, or a suspected food safety incident.

This page's slug corresponds to a handbook occupational group name, but this round's selected modules concern O*NET35-3023.00 Fast Food and Counter Workers: taking orders and serving at counters or steam tables, potentially collecting payment and preparing simple food. The directory includes simple cooking, hotel room and in-car service, dining-area tidying, staff supervision and mentoring, and special-diet meals; all hot-food work or mentoring should not be excluded. Full cook duties, table service, and business management are adjacent responsibility distinctions; occupational classification does not determine statutory licenses or shop authority.

entries: Orders and payments | Taking orders and settlement | Greet customers, take orders, repeat additions and allergen alerts for confirmation, and use checkout equipment to calculate prices, collect payments, give change, and check orders.

Assembly and service | Serving and packaging | Retrieve food from service or storage areas and plate or package it according to orders, check main items, drinks, and sides, and deliver promptly while observing service time limits.

Simple preparation | Beverages and light food | Mix cold drinks and milkshakes, brew coffee and tea, prepare simple foods such as sandwiches and salads, operate equipment as instructed, and control portions.

Food safety and temperature | Storage and time limits | Follow procedures for hot holding and cold-drink refrigeration, check food temperatures, separate raw and cooked foods, change gloves, and observe shelf-life and storage limits.

Cleaning and hygiene | Equipment and dining areas | Clean surfaces, counters, beverage equipment, and utensils, sweep and mop floors, wash dishes, set up and clear dining areas, and maintain sanitary facilities.

Inventory and collaboration | Restocking and mentoring | Monitor and request food and supplies, replenish promptly, report shortages and special orders to supervisors, and collaborate and mentor new colleagues as assigned.

paragraphs:
Work context | O*NET 35-3023.00 indicates public-facing work, fast-paced repetitive labor, and teamwork; conditions vary with shop type, shift, and customer traffic.
Constant contact | Constant contact with others (89%), requiring ongoing communication with customers and colleagues during peaks.
Teamwork | Working with others is extremely important (86%); counter and kitchen teams must coordinate closely.
Customer emotions | Daily handling of unpleasant, angry, or discourteous people (78%); conflict once a week or more but not daily (42%).
Decision freedom | Considerable decision freedom 73%; considerable freedom to determine tasks and priorities 43%, within standard procedures.
Movements and posture | Continual or almost continual repetitive motions (64%) and standing (54%); bending or twisting about half the time (57%).
Physical proximity | Very close proximity to others (48% very close), with crowded peak-period spaces.
Accuracy and repetition | Exactness or accuracy is extremely important (50%); repeating the same task is extremely important (54%).
Risk exposure | Daily exposure to situations involving minor burns and cuts (29%, not an actual injury rate); controlled indoor environments (68% daily).

Environment and pace | Shops are mostly indoors with controlled environments (O*NET 68% daily), but counters are close to hot holding tables, frying and beverage equipment, and refrigerated areas, with marked temperature and humidity changes. Customer traffic fully drives the pace: lunch and dinner rushes, holidays, and promotions require continuous standing, quick movement, and frequent repetition, with constant trips between kitchen and counter. Shifts include early mornings, evenings, weekends, and holidays; some shops require rotations and unplanned overtime. Physical demands center on prolonged standing and walking, repeatedly moving goods and water containers, dishwashing, and mopping. Follow procedures to prevent slips and protect against hot surfaces.

Tools and materials | Equipment: checkout and order terminals, beverage and coffee machines, milkshake and ice cream machines, simple heating equipment such as steam tables and fryers, food thermometers, dishwashers and cleaning tools (mops, cloths, disinfectants), and waste and recycling containers. Materials: food ingredients, wrapping paper and meal containers, utensils and straws, disposable gloves and hairnets. Information: shop standard procedures and recipe cards, food safety and hygiene procedures, temperature and time records, allergen and ingredient lists, schedules, and end-of-shift reconciliation forms. All food safety parameters (holding and refrigeration temperatures, storage limits, disinfectant concentrations) must follow the procedures and product instructions valid for the shift.

Greet and take orders → Repeat additions and allergens for confirmation → Calculate prices, collect payment, and give change → Assemble, package, and check → Deliver and restock as needed → Clean and reconcile shift-end accounts

Quality standards | Orders should match customer selections (correct items, additions, no-ice requests, and allergen notes), with timely service and temperatures meeting procedures. Payments and change must be accurate, and shift-end accounts balanced. Food must meet hygiene requirements: maintain hot holding and cold-drink refrigeration temperatures, separate raw and cooked foods, change gloves and disinfect surfaces as required, and handle food beyond storage limits according to procedures. Discuss and record any mismatch with recipe cards, hygiene procedures, or customer notes with the shift supervisor first; do not independently lower standards or ignore allergen alerts.

Adjacent responsibility boundaries | This page covers O*NET-SOC 35-3023.00. Adjacent but distinct occupations include Waiters and Waitresses (orders and dine-in service in formal restaurants), Cooks, Fast Food (mainly cooking and meal preparation), Food Preparation Workers (mainly ingredient preprocessing), Cashiers (mainly payments and settlement), Dishwashers (mainly cleaning utensils and equipment), and First-Line Supervisors of Food Preparation and Serving Workers (scheduling and on-site management). These differ in objects, techniques, authority, and responsibilities. Menu development, equipment repair, food safety incident determinations, and statutory hygiene inspections belong to relevant roles and authorities; this occupation does not replace their judgment or sign-off.

Boundary review points | Pause and escalate when: a customer raises a potentially severe allergen requirement and ingredients cannot be confirmed; equipment failure affects temperature control or food safety; suspected food safety incidents occur (unusual smells, discoloration, abnormal temperatures); customers become intensely upset, abusive, or physically threatening; payments and accounts show major discrepancies; or cancellation, discount, and compensation requests exceed authority. The shift supervisor, shop manager, or relevant authority handles these under procedures and laws.
Take orders → Confirm and price → Collect payment and give change → Assemble and package → Deliver and restock → Clean and reconcile

Difference from waiters-and-waitresses (Waiters and Waitresses): They take orders, serve dishes, and provide dine-in service in formal restaurants, usually involving drinks and table service. This occupation mainly works in fast food and counter settings, emphasizing rapid orders, assembly and serving, and payment collection; service formats and processes differ.

Difference from cooks-fast-food (Cooks, Fast Food): They focus on cooking and meal preparation, including frying, heating, and producing meals. This occupation mainly handles counter orders, assembly and service, and payments, preparing simple food and beverages only as needed. Work locations and main responsibilities differ.

Difference from food-preparation-workers (Food Preparation Workers): They mainly wash, cut, and preprocess ingredients, usually in the kitchen. This occupation directly serves customers through orders, service, payments, and shop hygiene, with more frequent customer contact and greater communication requirements.

Difference from cashiers (Cashiers): They mainly scan goods, settle payments, and process returns and exchanges across retail shops. In addition to payment collection, this occupation takes food orders, assembles and serves meals, and follows food safety and cleaning procedures, with broader duties.

Before choosing this occupation, compare actual tasks (proportions of counter service, simple preparation, cleaning, and restocking), qualification and training routes (on-the-job training, food safety and hygiene training, and beverage service training in some regions), shifts and physical demands (early and late shifts, weekends and holidays, prolonged standing, and repetitive motions), health and safety costs (hot surfaces and fryers, cuts and slips, and customer conflict), and progression (moving to waiting, fast food cooking, food preparation, or shop supervision). Chains and regions differ considerably; check actual vacancies and shop observations.

Responsibility boundaries cannot be inferred from similar job titles. Among food-service roles, counter service, formal restaurant service, cooking, ingredient preprocessing, checkout, and dishwashing differ in objects, locations, techniques, and authority. Cross-role work requires learning processes and food safety procedures anew; judgment and sign-off authority do not carry over. Equipment maintenance and food safety incident handling must be performed by the relevant responsible parties.

AI task exposure | Digital tools may assist self-service and QR-code ordering, order displays and queue management, inventory and supply reminders, scheduling and shift-end reconciliation records, simple customer questions, and content drafts. Shop staff remain responsible for on-site order taking and confirmation, assembly and service, food safety and temperature judgments, customer emotions, and abnormality escalation. Task exposure does not equal job replacement.

Adoption conditions | Shop digital tools must produce traceable, reviewable outputs without replacing actual on-site judgment of food and equipment; reminders and records must not displace service and cleaning time; and records involving orders, cancellations, discounts, and accounts require shift-supervisor confirmation before settlement. A technical demonstration does not establish organizational adoption or change food safety and hygiene responsibilities.

Data and system prerequisites | Before adoption, check whether order and payment records trace to original orders; inventory and near-expiry reminder definitions and update frequency; access permissions and retention periods for customer and payment information; degraded operation during network or equipment failure; consistency between self-ordering and kitchen displays; and traceable grounds for automatic recommendations and allergen alerts.

Human control points and review | Shop staff and shift supervisors must confirm orders and allergens, judge food temperatures and time limits, separate raw and cooked food, clean and disinfect, handle customer emotions, and escalate abnormalities. Tool-generated orders, reminders, inventory findings, and reconciliation conclusions require human review and retained evidence before use.

Remaining responsibilities | Matters that must not be automatically approved include whether food is safe to serve (temperature, time limits, suspected contamination), suspected allergen cross-contact risks, cancellations and discounts, and decisions involving customer safety and hygiene compliance. No tool output constitutes a finding of acceptability or authorization.

Failure risks | Unreviewed tool outputs may cause incorrect orders and allergen information, distorted inventory and near-expiry reminders, reconciliation errors, or on-site use of unconfirmed recommendations and substitutions as established plans, causing customer complaints, food safety risks, and shop losses. Before implementation, specify who reviews outputs and which original information they use.

Employment evidence boundaries | Distinguish statistical scopes for this occupation's employment and wage data. US O*NET and BLS figures are estimates under specific definitions and cannot be directly extrapolated to mainland China or other regions. Chinese industry average wages provide background proxies, not occupational wage conclusions. All generated content should trace to original inputs and sources; fluent wording is not evidence of correctness.

Practical response | First use digital tools in reversible, auditable, low-risk steps (such as order organization, inventory and near-expiry records, scheduling and reconciliation assistance), subject to shift-supervisor confirmation and actual operations. Decide whether to expand use based on errors and customer feedback; food safety and service judgments must always retain human confirmation.

Cross-market statistical boundaries | Mainland China and the United States use different industry and occupational classification systems. Mainland China publishes average wages of employees in urban units by national economic industry category without separate figures for this occupation; the United States provides SOC occupational and industry estimates. The two cannot be combined or converted, and industry averages cannot replace occupational wages.

Insufficient evidence: Mainland China has not established public occupational wage statistics precisely matching Fast Food and Counter Workers; industry averages, advertised pay, and third-party estimates are not substituted.

Mainland China wage evidence review points | This page provides only statistical definitions, industry background proxies, and visible gap records, without estimated occupational pay. Before using figures, confirm whether statistical scope (industry category / occupation), period, units, and covered population are comparable with this occupation.

US wage evidence review points | US figures come from BLS OEWS May 2025 and BLS 2024—2034 Employment Projections (presented through O*NET). Before use, confirm occupational scope (SOC 35-3023), inclusion of tips and bonuses (OEWS includes tips and some bonuses but excludes benefits and overtime premiums), and national rather than specific regional or employer scope.

Mainland China wage evidence—market scope | The National Bureau of Statistics publishes average wages of employees in urban units by industry category, covering urban units nationwide without occupational breakdowns. Relevant categories such as accommodation and food services provide background only and cannot replace occupational wages. Employment arrangements vary considerably among chain shops, independent restaurants, and canteens and are difficult for public statistics to cover.
Insufficient evidence: No mainland China median wage for fast food and counter workers verifiable by occupation has been obtained; industry-category averages are not substituted.

Mainland China wage evidence—statistical period | Industry average wages are annual figures (the figures below are for 2025, published in 2026), unlike the US May 2025 wage reference point on this page. The periods must not be mixed.

Cross-market statistical boundaries | Mainland China industry average wages and US occupational wages differ in statistical subjects, periods, and definitions. This page presents them separately with limitations, without exchange-rate conversion or treating industry averages as occupational wages.

Mainland China wage evidence—units | The National Bureau of Statistics reports annual average wages in yuan / year, using total pre-tax wages (including individual income tax and employee social insurance and housing provident fund contributions withheld by employers). US OEWS reports dollars / hour or dollars / year; this occupation includes tips and some bonuses but excludes overtime premiums and benefits. Units and included components differ and cannot be directly compared.

Insufficient evidence: No mainland China wages for fast food and counter workers verifiable by region or employment arrangement have been obtained; individual offers and secondhand accounts are not substituted.

Mainland China wage evidence—covered population | Urban non-private unit statistics cover employees of non-private legal entities in urban areas, while urban private unit statistics cover private-unit employees. Neither covers individually owned businesses, freelancers, or casual employment. Part-time, hourly, and peak-season temporary arrangements common in food service differ substantially and are difficult for public statistics to cover.

US wage evidence—market scope | BLS OEWS provides sample-survey estimates representing employer-reported wages, including tips and some bonuses but excluding the self-employed. The median is the distribution midpoint, not starting pay or the level at a particular region or employer.

US wage evidence—statistical period | Wages are from May 2025 OEWS; employment, growth, and openings are from 2024—2034 Employment Projections. These data types have different reference points and must not be combined as conclusions for a single point in time.

US wage evidence—units | Published in dollars / hour and dollars / year. Annual mean wages are converted to a full-year full-time basis; converting hourly and annual figures does not establish personal actual income, which also depends on hours, shifts, tips, and seasonality.

US wage evidence—covered population | Covers employees reported by nonfarm establishment employers, excluding self-employment, some family operations, and unreported cash-paid work. Food service has many part-time, hourly, and peak-season casual workers, which public statistics struggle to fully reflect.

US wage evidence—occupational scope | Figures correspond to SOC 35-3023 (Fast Food and Counter Workers), excluding waiters and waitresses (35-3031), fast food cooks (35-2014), food preparation workers (35-2021), cashiers (41-2011), and dishwashers (35-9021). Wages across occupations must not be mixed.

US wage evidence—sampling and missing-data limitations | OEWS sample estimates have sampling error, and industry and regional breakdowns may have missing or unreliable estimates. This occupation has very large employment (about 3,796,000 in 2024, the BLS occupational projection base year, presented through O*NET), but chain and independent shops differ greatly, and detailed industry estimates may still be missing. This page has not obtained industry wages readable by industry and records a visible gap; industry averages and third-party estimates are not substituted.

paragraphs: Conclusion | The core differences concern what workers mainly do in the shop, where they work, and whom they face. This occupation takes counter orders, assembles and serves food, collects payments, and performs hygiene and restocking duties. Waiters provide table orders and service in formal restaurants; fast food cooks cook and prepare meals in kitchens; food preparation workers preprocess ingredients; cashiers mainly settle product payments; dishwashers mainly clean utensils and equipment. Locations, customer-contact frequency, and authority differ; judgment and sign-off authority cannot carry across roles.

Evidence note | Comparisons below come from O*NET occupational classifications and publicly available sales information, helping distinguish adjacent occupations' work and suitable choices without establishing qualifications, hiring, or pay. Check each occupation's wages and employment separately under its own SOC scope. The table does not compare figures or use one occupation's wages as a proxy for another.

Introduction | The comparison uses four columns: occupational direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and choices it better suits. Adjacent roles collaborate closely within a shop (counter, kitchen, and washing areas connect), but are not interchangeable. Moving between directions requires learning processes, food safety procedures, and equipment operation anew.
Centers on counter orders, assembly and service, payments, and shop hygiene, emphasizing fast order taking, accurate checks, food safety and temperature control, and customer communication.

Better suited to people who remain steady at a fast peak-period pace, willingly interact frequently with customers, and follow standard procedures; acceptance of repetitive motions and changing schedules supports a closer fit.
Outputs are shop service results: order confirmation, assembly and packaging, payments and change, serving and restocking, cleaning, and shift-end reconciliation.
This occupation: Fast Food and Counter Workers
Centers on table orders, serving, and dine-in service in formal restaurants, usually involving multiple-course pacing and beverage service, multiple customers per table, and complex orders and bills.
Better suited to people wanting more customer interaction and able to remember complex menus and table arrangements; those preferring rapid counter turnover may choose this occupation.
Outputs are dine-in services: greeting and orders, serving and clearing plates, beverage service, bills, and tip settlement.
Waiters and Waitresses
Centers on frying, heating, and meal production in the kitchen, emphasizing equipment operation, serving speed, and consistent taste; mainly kitchen-based.
Better suited to people willing to focus on cooking and equipment and tolerate kitchen heat and a physically demanding pace; those preferring direct customer contact suit this occupation.
Outputs are meals: ingredient preparation and preprocessing, frying and heating, plating and serving, equipment cleaning and care.
Cooks, Fast Food
Centers on washing, cutting, and preprocessing ingredients for cooking and serving, mainly repetitive preparation with little customer contact.
Better suited to people preferring quiet preparation and procedural work rather than frequent customer contact.
Outputs are prepared ingredients and semifinished foods: inspection and storage, washing and cutting, portioning and shelf-life records.
Food Preparation Workers

Centers on product scanning, payment settlement, and returns and exchanges, working with goods and orders and emphasizing payment accuracy and loss prevention, usually without food preparation or service.
Better suited to people preferring standard payment processes without handling food and equipment; those wanting food service alongside payments suit this occupation.
Outputs are payment results: scanning and pricing, payments and change, returns and discounts, and shift-end reconciliation.
Cashiers
Centers on washing and returning utensils, cookware, and equipment, emphasizing hygiene and efficiency, with essentially no customer contact and work in washing areas.
Better suited to people preferring independent washing and organizing and able to accept wet, hot environments.
Outputs are clean utensils and equipment: sorting and soaking, washing and sanitizing, returning and checking, and washing-area maintenance.
Dishwashers

Transition | This page places adjacent roles side by side by responsibility and location to help decide which shop work you want to pursue long term. Whatever direction you choose, work readiness depends on understanding standard procedures and food safety, stable performance under peak pressure, and practical assessment recognized by employers or shift supervisors. Interest questionnaires only raise questions.

What personality suits this work? Emotional steadiness, responsibility, and willingness to communicate matter more than a particular type. O*NET interest code CRS (Conventional—Realistic—Social) can be an exploration starting point.

Can introverted people fit? They can adapt. Counter and kitchen coordination mainly uses brief, procedural communication, but you must actively confirm orders and requirements. If facing customer emotions is extremely difficult, consider kitchen or washing roles.

What should I prepare before entry? Understand actual shop pace (continuous peak-period standing, repetitive motions, early and late shifts, and holidays), and basic food safety and hygiene. You can start as a counter helper or hourly worker.
Unpleasant customers: 78% daily; conflict: 42% weekly, not daily. These are not actual violence or injury and illness rates.

Are there physical requirements? Prolonged standing and walking, moving goods, and equipment operation are required. Specific employment and medical examination requirements depend on employers and local laws; this page provides no medical examination conclusions.

US occupational education: 56% below high school / 24% high school / 17% some college without a degree; BLS typically requires no formal education. JobZone1—2 is a general preparation description; check Chinese announcements separately.

Can long-term work harm health? Prolonged standing, repetitive movements, hot surfaces and fryers, cuts, and slippery floors are practical costs. Use protective equipment, take work breaks, and follow procedures.

Career progression and transitions? Progress from counter work and assistance to skilled service, shift supervision, and shop management, or move to waiting, fast food cooking, food preparation, barista work, or checkout. Moving between directions requires relearning processes and procedures.

How can I test fit? Use a real or simulated peak-period shop task: Can you maintain accurate orders and serving speed under pressure, accept repetitive labor and shifts, and handle customer emotions appropriately?

Caution signals: Difficulty accepting frequent customer contact and emotional conflict, prolonged standing and repetitive labor, or early, late, and holiday shifts.
Validation suggestion: Use a simulated or actual shop peak task to test movement speed, order accuracy, and emotional steadiness before deciding on long-term commitment.

entries.answer: Under O*NET-SOC 35-3023.00, workers take orders and serve food and beverages at counters or steam tables, collect payments, and may prepare simple food and drinks (such as sandwiches, salads, soups, pizza, coffee, and cold drinks). Work includes orders and confirmation, assembly and packaging, payments and change, simple preparation, temperature and time controls, cleaning and hygiene, restocking, and shift-end reconciliation. It excludes full hot-dish kitchen cooking and menu development, formal restaurant dine-in service, shop operations management decisions, and checkout-system financial master-data design.
entries.question: What exactly does this occupation do?

entries.answer: Waiters handle table orders, serving, and beverages in formal restaurants; fast food cooks handle kitchen cooking and preparation; food preparation workers preprocess ingredients; cashiers focus on product settlement; dishwashers clean utensils and equipment. This occupation takes counter orders, assembles and serves food, collects payments, and performs shop hygiene and restocking, with frequent direct customer contact and standard procedures. Locations and responsibility boundaries differ.

Rotation, protection, and breaks can reduce strain, but prolonged standing, repetition, and heat-source risks remain practical costs.

entries.answer: Effects mainly concern records, schedules, and self-service: tools may assist self-ordering and QR-code ordering, order displays and queues, inventory and near-expiry reminders, scheduling and reconciliation, and simple customer questions. Shop staff and shift supervisors retain on-site order and allergen confirmation, assembly and service, temperature and time controls, customer emotions, and abnormality escalation. entries.answer: Training, certification, employer appointment, and scheduling, discount, and food safety handling authority are four different states. entries.answer: Common failures include inadequate temperature and time control, raw and cooked cross-contamination and mishandled allergens, burns and cuts from hot surfaces, fryers, and knives, customer conflict outside procedures, payment, cancellation, and reconciliation errors, and slippery floors, lifting, and repetitive-motion strain. Key controls are following procedures and keeping records, pausing, and escalating.
